secular oscillations in the Mg/Co ratio of seawater, driven by tectonic changes in the spreading rates of mid-ocean ridings, have controlled the carbonate mineralogy and the biological composition of reef-building and bioclastic-producing organisms throughout the Phaneroozoic Eon.

the mineralogy of hypercalcareous organisms and their sedimentary products oscillate in a predictable manner in response to secular changes in the chemistry of seawater.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of tectonic processes in driving secular changes in the mineralogy and ecology of marine carbonate systems.
the evolution of the Earth's surface environment and the evolution of life in the Phaneroozoic Era, and with the interaction between the two.
the evolution of reef ecosystems, with the evolution of the carbonate rock record, and with the evolution of seawater chemistry.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Mg/Ca of seawater has been the most powerful control of reef and carbonate sediment composition during the Phaneroozoic.

the Mg/Ca ratios of seawater have controlled the mineralogy of reef builders and sediment producers and that these ratios have been strongly influenced by the spreading rate along mid-ocean ridge systems.

the mineralogical composition of carbonate skeletons and sediments, and hence the mineralogical character of carbonate rocks, has been strongly controlled by variations in the chemistry of the oceans, which have been driven by variations in the rate of seafloor spreading.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Mg/Ca of seawater has been the primary determinant of carbonate mineralogy in the oceans, and thus of carbonate deposition and preservation, for the last 600 million years.
the carbonate mineralogy and composition of marine organisms is strongly influenced by the Mg/Ca ratios of seawater.

the carbonate mineralogy and the biological composition of reef tracts and carbonate deposits have been driven by secular oscillations in the Mg/Co ratio of seawater, which in turn has been controlled by changes in the spreading rates of mid-ocean ridged driven by changes in the rate of plate motion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in addition to being a powerful tool for deciphering the history of the Earth's surface and interior, carbonate mineralogy can be used to decipher the history of life.
the mineralogy of reef building and sediment producing organisms is strongly controlled by seawater chemistry.
the Mg/Ca of seawater is the primary driver of the mineralogy of carbonate sediments and reef communities, and this is a function of spreading rates along the mid-ocean ridging system.
